headline: Medium data-leakage and cascading-error risks: Khoj can read indexed files while Argo Workflows can move artifacts over allowlisted network paths, creating a plausible default-pathway for sensitive content to be surfaced and reused.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented, so a default prompt-injection bridge is not proven. However, Khoj reads indexed documents and Argo Workflows handles artifacts/parameters, so if an operator manually passes Argo outputs into Khoj, malicious content could be reinterpreted as instructions. The pathway is indirect and requires unusual bridging.
conditions: IF Argo outputs are copied into Khoj-indexed notes or chat context
IF indexed documents contain attacker-controlled instructions
mitigations: Keep Argo outputs out of Khoj’s indexed corpus
Label workflow artifacts as untrusted before ingestion
Use a separate review step for any copied output
Restrict indexing to curated folders only

B_data_leakage.rationale: Khoj explicitly reads indexed personal notes/files and may use cloud or self-hosted servers, while Argo Workflows touches artifacts and parameters with allowlisted network egress. In a shared workspace, sensitive content can flow from Argo-produced artifacts into Khoj’s retrieval corpus and then into model outputs. This is plausible in default usage, though not directly evidenced as a forced leak.
conditions: IF Argo artifacts contain sensitive parameters or outputs
IF those artifacts are indexed or opened by Khoj
IF Khoj is configured to query a remote model provider
mitigations: Exclude workflow artifact directories from Khoj indexing
Separate sensitive Argo runs from personal-note repositories
Use self-hosted inference for Khoj where possible
Rotate any secrets that appear in workflow outputs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Argo Workflows can call APIs and use allowlisted network egress, while Khoj has broad network egress and reads files but cannot write files or modify git state. Their write surfaces do not overlap, so direct resource contention is limited. The main conflict is read-side interference over shared files or APIs, which is smaller than a mutable-state clash.
conditions: IF both agents target the same external API quota
IF both read the same files while one is being regenerated
mitigations: Stagger API-heavy jobs and chat queries
Use separate service accounts per agent
Avoid sharing mutable directories between them
Add rate limits on shared upstream APIs

D_cascading_error.rationale: Khoj’s retrieval/chat layer can treat indexed documents as authoritative context, and Argo Workflows can generate artifacts or parameters that later become those documents. If Argo emits incorrect outputs, Khoj may surface them without verification, causing downstream decisions to inherit the error. The pair lacks a built-in verification boundary in the profiles, so the cascade is plausible.
conditions: IF Argo-generated artifacts are ingested into Khoj
IF Khoj answers are used as operational guidance without human review
mitigations: Require human review before indexing workflow outputs
Tag workflow-generated content as untrusted
Add source citations in Khoj responses
Quarantine failed or partial Argo runs from retrieval

E_compliance.rationale: Khoj stores personal notes/files and model-provider API keys for self-hosted use, while Argo Workflows handles artifacts and parameters with allowlisted egress. If personal or regulated data from Argo workflows is indexed into Khoj, retention and residency obligations can diverge across the two systems. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so this is a policy-gap risk rather than a confirmed breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in Argo artifacts
IF those artifacts are retained in Khoj indexes beyond the source system’s policy
mitigations: Define a shared retention policy for both systems
Exclude regulated datasets from Khoj indexing
Document data residency for any remote model calls
Purge indexed copies when source artifacts expire
